evals.prompt: I'm head of DevRel at Tarnhelm, we sell a hosted feature-flag platform to engineering orgs. The board question for FY27 is why five of our top ten accounts have 200+ developers on the platform but flags are still 'that team's tool' instead of the company standard - renewals at two of those accounts are pinned to us becoming the org-wide default. Sales ops already built full account rollup in our CRM, and product telemetry covers SDK init and first flag evaluation. Our internal wiki has a diagram someone drew in 2024 going discover -> try -> adopt -> contribute -> advocate. Can you put together a proper developer journey map for us? Segment is platform engineers at 1000+ person companies, and I need it before planning closes in three weeks.
evals.expected_output: A stage-model selection pass that names standardisation as the funded end state, deletes the models whose terminal stage is not standardisation, recommends Revell's six-stage model while explaining that the pre-built account rollup cancels most of its usual cost, and stops for the user's choice before any row is written.
expectations: Names the funded end state as organisation-wide standardisation before proposing any stage model.
Deletes candidate stage models whose terminal stage is not standardisation, rather than ranking all of them.
Records which models were deleted and why in the map's Scope section.
Recommends Revell's six-stage model.
Lists Revell's stages: initial awareness, deep awareness, evaluation and validation, commitment, standardization, community and advocacy.
Attributes the six-stage model to Matthew Revell, developerrelations.com, 2016.
States that Revell's is the only published model carrying an explicit standardisation stage.
Notes Revell normally costs on the order of a quarter, because its standardisation boundary needs account rollup and buyer-side interviews.
Explicitly re-ranks Revell upward because Tarnhelm already has account rollup built for sales, which removes most of that cost.
Offers two or three candidate models with what each makes visible and what it hides, and asks the user to choose before writing rows.
Does not blend the existing discover -> try -> adopt -> contribute -> advocate spine with a published model.
Identifies discover -> try -> adopt -> contribute -> advocate as an unsourced default rather than a published framework.
Does not produce filled stage rows before the stage model is agreed.

evals.prompt: Quick sanity check before I take this to our VP of Product. Northwind Streams sells a managed Kafka alternative. Last quarter 28% of people who started our quickstart made a first successful produce-and-consume call, and 22% of signups hit what we internally call activation (a topic created plus one message consumed within 7 days). I keep seeing 40-60% quoted as the normal quickstart conversion for API products, and 20-40% as the standard self-serve activation rate, so on both counts we look broken. I want the journey map to open with those two gaps so the VP immediately sees the size of the problem. Segment is backend engineers at Series-A to Series-C startups, end state is production usage.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to benchmark 28% and 22% against the quoted figures, an explanation that circulating per-stage rates are incompatible single-company anecdotes, a correct account of what the real published activation numbers are and are not, and a map that carries Northwind's own rates with their definitions.
expectations: Refuses to use the 40-60% quickstart conversion figure as a benchmark.
Refuses to use the 20-40% self-serve activation figure as a benchmark.
States that circulating per-stage conversion figures are single-company anecdotes with incompatible stage definitions.
States that no normal discovery-to-production rate for a developer product can be quoted.
States that the only honest comparison is against this same map's own previous version.
Does not open the map with a benchmark-gap framing.
Notes that the leading developer-tools product benchmark survey declines to publish a single activation-rate figure, because the activation milestone differs by product.
Names a real published activation figure with its methodology when discussing activation at all, for example the self-reported 25% median / 34% average survey band, and labels it self-reported.
Distinguishes that self-reported activation band from instrumented day-7 return figures (about 2.1% median, 7% top quartile) as different metrics under different definitions.
States that the popular round 20-40% figure collapses two different metrics into one number.
Records 28% and 22% in the map as Northwind's own numbers, with their definitions stated.
States that Northwind's activation definition (topic created plus one message consumed in 7 days) is product-specific and not comparable to another company's milestone.
Does not declare either stage broken on the strength of a borrowed rate.

evals.prompt: We're mapping the journey for Cindershell, a CLI-first infrastructure tool. Segment is SREs at mid-market companies, end state is production usage. I pulled Google Analytics for our docs site: 14,200 sessions last month, and 61% of them show as 'direct'. Our agency says a direct share that big means the tracking is broken and wants a six-week instrumentation project before we do anything else with the funnel. I'd like the awareness and evaluation rows of the map to carry those session numbers so we have something concrete at the top.
evals.expected_output: A map that refuses to write absolute docs traffic into cells, explains analytics blocking and referrer loss with their sources and caveats, labels the early stages inferred, and proceeds now with the instrumentation need recorded in Gaps rather than blocking on a six-week project.
expectations: Declines to write the 14,200 absolute session count into any stage cell.
Cites the measurement that 58% of a tech audience blocks third-party analytics scripts.
Attributes that figure to Plausible Analytics' August 2021 measurement, and notes it is a single-site measurement by an interested vendor.
Gives at least one sub-breakdown from that measurement: 82.3% on Linux, 88.3% on Firefox, or 68.2% desktop versus 49.9% mobile.
States that the blocking rate varies page by page, so absolute developer-surface traffic is wrong by a factor that changes per page.
States that only ratios inside a single source survive.
States that a large 'direct' bucket is the normal case for a developer audience, not an instrumentation bug.
Notes roughly 70% of AI-assistant-driven traffic arrives with no referrer, and labels that as a newsletter estimate rather than a study.
Labels the awareness and evaluation stages as inferred wherever they appear in the map.
Declines to block the map on the six-week instrumentation project.
Puts the instrumentation need in the map's Gaps section.
Orders any proposed instrumentation fixes by cost: first-party or proxied script, then server or CDN log analysis, then a product-side event for anything past signup.
Does not recommend chasing the direct bucket down to a smaller share.

evals.prompt: Building the journey map for Orrery - an open-source Python data-quality library plus a paid cloud. Segment is data engineers, end state is production usage of the cloud. For the discovery and evaluation rows I want a year-over-year view: GitHub clones and unique visitors for the last 12 months. I also want our npm downloads (we ship a small JS companion) put next to our PyPI downloads so we can show which ecosystem is adopting us faster. And our all-time download counter just crossed 4.1M, which I'd like as the headline discovery signal.
evals.expected_output: A correction that repository traffic data expired long ago and cannot be backfilled, the retention windows for each registry, why npm and PyPI counts are not comparable and are not people, a rejection of the all-time counter, and the missing baseline recorded in Gaps.
expectations: States that repository traffic endpoints retain only 14 days of data.
Notes those endpoints require write access to the repository.
States that expired repository traffic data cannot be backfilled, so a 12-month view is not available.
Instructs snapshotting any signal drawn from an expiring source into the team's own store from the day the signal is defined.
States npm download data retains 18 months.
States PyPI time series retain 180 days.
States npm counts HTTP 200 responses for tarballs, including build servers and mirrors, making it a request count rather than a person count.
States PyPI excludes known mirrors by default.
Concludes npm and PyPI download counts are not comparable to each other, and that neither is a user count.
Declines to present the requested year-over-year repository traffic comparison as achievable from existing data.
Rejects the 4.1M all-time download counter as a signal because it is monotonic and cannot fall when the journey breaks.
Proposes a rate or a period delta in place of the all-time counter.
Places the missing historical baseline in the map's Gaps section.

evals.prompt: Mapping the journey for Pallasgate, an authorization-as-a-service API. 340 signups last quarter on the free tier, 9 closed deals. The developer is definitely not the one signing - our deals go through a security review and then procurement, averaging about three months. Segment is backend engineers at 500-5000 person companies, end state is paid conversion. Right now our funnel view is just 340 signups flowing to 9 deals, which makes the conversion look catastrophic and I get asked about it every board meeting. Give me the journey map.
evals.expected_output: A two-lane map: the developer lane plus a separate buyer lane with its own exit events and owners, gated on rolling usage up to accounts first, with the depth/spread/boundary-contact families named in intent order and boundary contact instrumented first.
expectations: Adds a second, shorter buyer lane alongside the developer lane rather than one merged funnel.
States that the developer lane counts people while the buyer lane counts organisations or accounts.
Requires usage to be rolled up to accounts before the buyer lane can be read at all.
Names at least one concrete rollup key: email domain, workspace or organisation object, licence or API key, or self-reported company.
States explicitly that the raw 340-to-9 comparison is unreadable without that rollup, because many signups from one company read as many leads.
Names the three buyer-lane signal families in increasing order of buying intent: depth, then spread, then boundary contact.
Defines spread as a second and third active developer inside the same account.

Gives at least two concrete boundary-contact examples, such as an SSO or RBAC page view, a compliance or audit question, a seat or rate limit hit, a security questionnaire request, or an enterprise terms page view.
Recommends instrumenting boundary contact first, and states it is the rarest and strongest of the three.
Gives the buyer lane its own exit events, such as security questionnaire cleared and contract signed.
Assigns the buyer lane's stages owners outside DevRel.
States the developer lane continues in parallel rather than ending where the buyer lane begins.
Records the champion as a participant carrying a specific artefact, not as a persona note.

evals.prompt:
Here is our stage table for Quillbore, a GraphQL gateway. Segment is backend engineers at scale-ups, end state is production usage. Stages are awareness -> onboarding -> integration -> production -> advocacy.

- Awareness: no owner, not instrumented
- Onboarding: 47% of quickstart starters reach first success, owned by our docs team
- Integration: 61% of first-success users call us from a service repo within 30 days, owned by product
- Production: 58% of integrating accounts reach 14-day sustained traffic, owned by product
- Advocacy: 3% of production accounts ever mention us publicly, owned by me (DevRel)

Advocacy is obviously our worst number by miles. I want the top three things to fix next quarter, and my read is that developers just aren't motivated enough to talk about us, so I'd like a motivation and incentive strategy for that stage.
evals.expected_output: Exactly one nominated leak - onboarding, not advocacy - chosen by recovered developers per unit of fix effort with earliest-and-owned as tiebreak, what that ordering starves and when advocacy gets promoted, and B=MAP applied only afterwards, to the chosen stage, with ability as the default branch.
expectations: Nominates exactly one leak, not three.
Nominates onboarding rather than advocacy.
States that the earliest leaking stage with an owner able to change it wins, because every downstream fix is diluted by the losses above it.
Ranks the candidate stages by developers recovered per unit of fix effort before applying the earliest-and-owned tiebreak.
Explicitly names what that ordering starves: a late stage with a large payoff and a heavy fix, here advocacy.
States the conditions that would promote advocacy anyway: the earliest leaking stage being unowned, its fix already in flight, or advocacy being the funded end state.
Does not apply B=MAP or any motivation analysis before the leak stage is chosen.
Applies B=MAP only to the chosen stage, naming motivation, ability and prompt.
Attributes B=MAP to BJ Fogg.
States that B=MAP explains one stage and cannot rank stages against each other.
Declines to deliver a motivation or incentive strategy for advocacy.
Names ability as the default branch for a developer audience and directs effort at raising ability rather than pumping motivation.
Flags that the awareness stage has no owner as a finding in its own right.

evals.prompt: Our CX team has a journey map template they use for our consumer app and they want us to reuse it for the developer side of Gravelock, a self-hosted observability agent. Segment is platform engineers, end state is production usage. Their template has columns for stage, customer goal, emotion score out of 10, pain points, and opportunities. The stage names they drafted for us are: developer becomes aware of need, developer understands the value proposition, developer feels confident in the product, developer commits, developer champions. Can you fill it in?
evals.expected_output: A rewritten row format with the eight required fields, emotion scores and the opportunities column refused with reasons, and every unobservable stage name converted into an observable event.
expectations: Refuses to include an emotion score column.
Gives the reason: emotion scores get invented at developer volumes and crowd out the columns carrying accountability.
Refuses to fill an opportunities column in the same pass as the map.
Gives the reason: writing opportunities in the same pass turns the map into a backlog before anyone knows which stage leaks.
Rejects 'developer understands the value proposition' as an exit event because it cannot be observed, counted or owned.
Rejects 'developer feels confident in the product' on the same grounds.
Replaces each unobservable stage name or exit criterion with a concrete observable event.
Names the eight fields a row carries: stage, developer's job, entry trigger, exit event, touchpoints, owner, friction evidence, signal.
Identifies exit event, owner and signal as the three fields without which a row is not finished.
Requires exactly one exit event per stage.
Requires exactly one signal per stage.
Writes the developer's job in the developer's own words rather than vendor funnel language.
Applies the test 'would a developer recognise this as something they did?' to each stage name.

evals.prompt: I maintain Thistlewrap, an MIT-licensed Go library for schema migrations, about 3,800 stars, used in production at a bunch of companies. I get maybe two outside PRs a quarter and almost every first-timer never comes back. I want a journey map that ends with people sticking around as contributors. Two side questions: I've been labelling issues 'easy' / 'medium' / 'hard' to help newcomers pick, and I'm not sure whether the map needs a buyer lane - companies run it in production but nobody pays us anything.
evals.expected_output: A map on the OSS contributor funnel with the merge as the contribution exit event, review latency as its signal, issue labels re-cut by API domain, and no buyer lane - with the adopting company's internal approval modelled as adoption-stage friction instead.
expectations: Selects the OSS contributor funnel as the stage model, because the funded end state is sustained contribution.
Names its stages: land, find work, set up, change, submit, survive review, return.
Identifies local setup and waiting for review as the two steps that leak hardest and most silently.
Sets the contribution stage's exit event as the merge, not the pull-request submission.
Cites the finding that contributors who received code review within 48 hours returned and contributed again at a much higher rate.
Attributes that finding to GitHub's Open Source Guides.
Proposes time-to-first-review as the contribution stage's signal.
Cites that it only takes one negative experience to make someone not want to come back.
States that newcomers pick tasks by the API domain a task requires rather than by a maintainer's difficulty label.
Attributes that finding to the newcomer-barriers study of 74 participants.
Recommends re-labelling issues by API domain or area rather than easy/medium/hard.
States there is no buyer lane on a project with no purchase, and says so explicitly on the map rather than leaving the lane blank.
Models the adopting company's internal approval - licence compatibility, dependency policy - as friction inside the adoption stage rather than as a lane.

evals.prompt: We did a journey map for Vaneworth last quarter, a CI runner service, using the five-stage API arc: awareness, onboarding, integration, production, advocacy. It was drawn for our 'indie and small team' segment. Three things for this refresh. One: update the numbers - onboarding went 34% to 39%, integration 52% to 49%, production 28% to 31%. Two: fold our enterprise platform-team audience into it so we have one map for everyone instead of maintaining two. Three: marketing standardised on AARRR company-wide this quarter, so switch us to AAARRRP so the vocabularies line up.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to merge the two segments, the five-stage arc kept for continuity over the AAARRRP switch, and a refresh that skips model selection and diffs each signal against its previous value.
expectations: Refuses to fold two audience segments into one map.
States the reason: a small-team path and an enterprise platform team's path are different journeys, so one map per segment.
Offers a second, separate map for the enterprise platform-team segment instead.
Keeps the five-stage API arc for this refresh rather than switching to AAARRRP.
States that on a refresh, comparability against the map's own history outranks a better-fitting vocabulary, and the model changes only if it actually broke.
Skips the stage-model selection step and goes straight to evidence collection for this refresh.
Diffs each signal against its previous value rather than restating only the current value.
Reports onboarding 34% to 39%, integration 52% to 49% and production 28% to 31% as movements against the previous map.
Names integration as the one stage whose rate moved backwards.
Compares only against this map's own previous version, not against any outside funnel.
Acknowledges the company-wide AARRR funnel as a genuine argument for AAARRRP, while subordinating it to continuity on a refresh.
States what would justify switching models later: the current model actually breaking.
Sets a re-read date, defaulting to 90 days and also triggered by a launch, a pricing change, a docs rewrite or a new SDK.

evals.prompt:
Signals for the Marrowfen journey map - embeddable charting SDK, segment is frontend engineers at product companies, end state production usage. Here is what I have, and I want a complete map with a number in every row, no blanks anywhere:

- Discover: total GitHub stars, 11,400
- Evaluate: nothing instrumented
- Try: cumulative signups, 22,900
- Adopt: nothing instrumented
- Contribute: nothing instrumented
- Advocate: 4 conference talks by non-employees last quarter, which I'd like expressed as 4 of 112 production accounts = 3.6%

Our company OKR this half is signups, so I want that one front and centre.
evals.expected_output: Monotonic counters rejected and converted, uninstrumented stages marked and listed in Gaps rather than filled, the signal-coverage gate reported as failed but the map shipped anyway, and the 4-event advocacy rate replaced by a dated raw list.
expectations: Rejects total GitHub stars as a signal because it is a monotonic counter that cannot fall when the stage breaks.
Rejects cumulative signups on the same grounds.
Converts each monotonic counter into a rate or a period delta.
Refuses to invent numbers for the uninstrumented stages.
Writes 'not instrumented' in those rows instead.
Lists the uninstrumented stages in the map's Gaps section.
States the gate that at least 60% of stages must carry a real current value, and reports that this map carries 2 of 6 and fails that line.
Ships the map anyway rather than blocking on the coverage gap.
States that an honest map with named holes beats a complete map with invented numbers.
Labels the 60% coverage figure as this skill's own working default rather than an industry standard.
Replaces the 3.6% advocacy rate with a dated raw list, because 4 events sit below the roughly-30-event floor.
Pairs the signups OKR with a quality counter-metric, such as 30-day retention of the same signup cohort.
Applies the 'so what' test and the ownership test to each proposed signal.

evals.prompt: Don't need a discovery phase on this one - the whole team already agrees the problem is our SDK reference docs, we've been saying it for about a year. Company is Halloway, a payments API. Segment is engineers at e-commerce platforms, end state production usage. Support barely ever gets tickets about onboarding, so that part is clearly fine. Just write the map with SDK docs as the leak and we'll take it from there.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to build the map from the team's belief, the SDK-docs theory recorded as a hypothesis, an evidence plan ordered cheapest-first with the friction log and exit interview protocols specified, and a correction of the inference that few onboarding tickets means onboarding works.
expectations: Declines to write the map from the team's existing belief.
States that a map assembled from opinion documents the team's beliefs, not the developer's path.
Records 'SDK reference docs' as the team's hypothesis rather than as friction evidence.
Orders evidence collection cheapest source first: walk the path and keep a friction log, mine what developers already wrote, interview developers, then read the funnel data that already exists.
Rejects the inference that few onboarding tickets means onboarding works.
States that developers who fail at setup rarely file anything, they leave.
Names the inverse signal: a stage with almost no questions and low conversion is a stage where people leave without speaking.
Specifies the friction log as one realistic scenario recorded as a running narrative, explicitly not minimal reproduction steps.
Requires the friction log to record verbatim search terms, clicked URLs and pasted commands, plus emotional reactions.
Names the green / yellow / red convention for delight, friction and blocking.
States that whoever is newest to the product makes the best friction logger.
Recommends interviewing 5 to 8 developers who completed the journey and 3 who abandoned it, and labels both counts as this skill's own defaults.
Instructs tagging each piece of evidence with the stage it belongs to before analysing it.

evals.prompt: Three things on my list for Sableworks, message-queue-as-a-service. Map the developer journey for our 'backend engineer at a scale-up' segment, end state production usage. Then rewrite our quickstart page so it converts better. And while you're in there, build me the DevRel KPI framework I have to present in November. Heads up on ownership: we're a three-person DevRel team and honestly we're the only ones who'd take any of these stages - docs, the dashboard, the SDK, community, all of it effectively lands on us because product is heads-down on the enterprise roadmap.
evals.expected_output: The journey map produced, the quickstart rewrite and the KPI framework declined and routed to the named sibling skills, and DevRel owning every row reported as an organisational finding that fails the gate without a fabricated owner being invented to pass it.
expectations: Produces the developer journey map.
Declines to rewrite the quickstart page as part of this run.
Routes the quickstart rewrite to samber/developer-relations-skills@developer-quickstart-guide by name.
Gives the reason for routing it out: a one-stage fix does not need a seven-stage artefact.
Declines to build the DevRel KPI framework as part of this run.
Routes the KPI framework to samber/developer-relations-skills@devrel-metrics by name.
Reports DevRel owning every row as a finding about the organisation, not merely a detail of the map.
States that it means the surfaces have no accountable owner, which is a bigger problem than the leak itself.
Names the gate line that at least one owner must sit outside the DevRel team, and reports this map failing it.
Does not fabricate an external owner in order to satisfy that gate.
Produces the deliverable under its seven headings: Scope, Journey, Buyer lane, Moments, Leak, Handoff, Gaps.
Names the three moments separately: first success, moment of truth, abandonment point.
Presents the document section by section for agreement rather than delivering it all at once.
